title: What are you doing?
goal: Talk about your daily activities, complete all three verb classes, and set up the rhythm rule — a sound rule no other European language has, which explains many endings that look wrong.
bekal: use all three Slovak verb classes and recognize the class from the *ja* form
describe your daily routine with time expressions
recognize and apply the rhythm rule

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bežný deň
dialogs.intro: Eva and Budi are waiting for the bus. The conversation turns to their routines.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: What do you do during the week?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ráno sa učím po slovensky a popoludní pracujem.

lines.text: V malej firme v centre. Píšem programy.

lines.text: To znie zaujímavo. A čo robíš večer?

notes: **Píšem, pracujem — the third class.** Its ending is *-em*, and it's the one that most often changes its stem: *písať → píšem* (s becomes š), *brať → beriem*, *ísť → idem*. The good news: the change is the same for all six persons, so you only need to learn the *ja* form and the rest flows.

**Verbs in -ovať always become -ujem.** *Pracovať → pracujem*, *študovať → študujem*, *kupovať → kupujem*, *ďakovať → ďakujem*. This is the most predictable group in all of Slovak, and it's huge — almost every modern borrowed verb joins it: *telefonovať, informovať, organizovať*.
**Sa učím, not učím.** The verb *učiť sa* always carries *sa*: literally "to teach oneself". Without *sa*, *učiť* means "to teach others". One little word reverses the direction of the action.

**Robievaš** is the habitual form — made by slipping in *-ieva-*, it means "to usually do, again and again". You don't need to produce it at A1, but recognize it when you hear it: *robiť → robievať*, *chodiť → chodievať*, *piť → pijavať*.
**Do hôr** = to the mountains. Notice *hora → hôr*: the vowel *o* lengthens to *ô* when the genitive plural ending disappears — exactly the pattern from unit 5.

grammars.title: The three verb classes — the full table
body: Every Slovak verb belongs to one of these three classes. The class is recognized from **the *ja* form**, not the dictionary form — that's why a good dictionary always lists both.
after: **The fourth column is really part of the third** — every *-ovať* verb is an *-em* verb with an inserted *-uj-*. It's shown separately because the group is large and its pattern is perfect.
**The last row is the one most often wrong**: *-ajú*, *-ia*, *-u*, *-ujú*. Four different endings for the same person. If you drill only one row of this table, drill this one.

**Irregular verbs** that must be learned separately: *byť* (som), *mať* (mám — actually regular), *jesť* (jem, ješ, je, jeme, jete, jedia), *ísť* (idem, ideš, ide, ideme, idete, idú), *vedieť* (viem, vieš, vie, vieme, viete, vedia), *chcieť* (chcem), *môcť* (môžem). Seven words, and all seven are used every day — so they'll stick on their own through use.

grammars.title: The rhythm rule — why endings are sometimes "wrong"
body: A rule no other Slavic language has, not even Czech, which is so close. It's simple: **two long syllables may not follow each other in one word**. If the syllable before is already long, an ending that should be long is shortened.

head: Base form
Expected ending
Result
Why
rows: *vo-* is short, the ending stays long
this ending is short anyway, unaffected

after: **What counts as long**: vowels with a mark (*á é í ó ú ý*), the glides (*ia ie iu*), *ô*, and *ŕ ĺ*. Everything else is short.

**Why does this matter now?** Because without this rule, half the endings you see in this course would look like typos. *Krásna* next to *pekná*, *prácam* next to *ženám* — both are correct, and the only difference is the length of the syllable before.

**At A1 you don't need to produce it perfectly.** What matters: don't "correct" what you see. If you write *krásná* because the pattern seems to call for it, a native speaker will instantly mark it as not Slovak — and as Czech.
**The exceptions are few and can be ignored for now**: some plural noun endings (*-ie*, *-ia*) and a few prefixes stay long even though they break the rule. You'll meet five at most in all of A1.

blocks.text: Notice how many end in **-ovať** and therefore take *-ujem*. This group keeps growing: almost every new word that enters Slovak from another language ends up here. *Googlovať → googlujem*. *Četovať → četujem*.

blocks.title: Verbs for meals
items: *Raňajky* (breakfast), *obed* (lunch), *večera* (dinner) are nouns, and all three have their own verbs: *raňajkovať, obedovať, večerať*. English needs two words ("have lunch"); Slovak has one.
*Obed* in Slovakia is the main meal of the day, usually between 11:30 and 1:00, and it almost always starts with soup. Turning down soup in a Slovak home needs a good excuse.

blocks.text: Time expressions usually stand **at the start of the sentence**, with the verb after them: *Ráno sa učím*, *Večer varím*, *Cez víkend chodím do hôr*. That order isn't required — Slovak word order is very free because the case endings already mark each word's role — but it sounds the most natural.

blocks.title: Nikdy demands a double negative
items: *Nikdy nepijem kávu.* — "I never drink coffee." Two negatives in one sentence, and both are required. *Nikdy pijem kávu* isn't just wrong; it means nothing.
The same rule applies to *nič* (nothing), *nikto* (nobody), *nikde* (nowhere): *Nič nevidím*, *Nikto tu nie je*, *Nikde ho nenájdem*.
What do you do during the week?
In the morning I study Slovak.
I usually read or watch films.
I eat in the canteen every day.
